class/GuiButton.d:
GuiButton is an abstract class that inherits from GuiObject. It is the base class for the interactive, clickable ImageButton and TextButton objects. This class also defines several properties for interactive behavior, namely AutoButtonColor and Modal.

The most important event of a GuiButton is Activated, a multi-platform event that fires when the button is activated. When using a mouse, this means clicking the button and releasing with the cursor still over the UI object. For touch, the same applies but with a touch instead of button press. Finally, for gamepads, Activated fires if a GuiButton is selected when the A button is pressed and released. In short, this event is very useful for multi-platform user interface programming as it provides a nice general interface for a single user input.
class/GuiButton.s: An abstract class for interactive 2D user interface elements.

m.d:
This property determines whether the button automatically changes color when the user's Mouse hovers over or clicks on it. If true, the button will automatically change color when the mouse hovers over or clicks on it. If false, the button will not change.

If you would like to customize how a button changes when the user's mouse hovers over or clicks on it, consider using an ImageButton and changing the element's HoverImage and PressedImage.

Please note that this property will not have an effect on an ImageButton if its Image property is set to an image. Additionally, this property will not affect an ImageButton on mouse hover when its HoverImage is not nil, nor on mouse click if its PressedImage is not nil.
m.s: Determines whether the button automatically changes color when the mouse hovers over or clicks on it.

kid.simple: When true (default), the button automatically gets a bit darker when you hover over or press it, so players can tell it's clickable. Set false if you want to make your own hover effect.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.AutoButtonColor = false -- I'll do my own hover colors
kid.gotcha: On an ImageButton with an Image set, this has no effect; use HoverImage and PressedImage instead.

m.d:
A HapticEffect that the engine plays the first time the pointer moves over the button, when the button transitions from its idle state to its hover state. Assign a HapticEffect to give hover feedback (for example, a light effect on gamepad or mobile); leave it unset for no hover haptics.

The effect plays through the standard HapticService mixer, so whether the player actually feels vibration depends on their device and haptic settings. This property defaults to nil (no effect).
m.s: A `Class.HapticEffect` instance that will play when the `Class.GuiButton` is being hovered.

kid.simple: A HapticEffect (vibration) that plays when the pointer first moves onto the button. Leave empty for no vibration. Whether the player feels it depends on their device and settings.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
local buzz = Instance.new("HapticEffect")
buzz.Type = Enum.HapticEffectType.UIHover
buzz.Parent = button
button.HoverHapticEffect = buzz

m.d: If true while the GUI element is visible, the mouse will not be locked unless the right mouse button is down.
m.s: If `true` while the GUI element is visible, the mouse will not be locked unless the right mouse button is down.

kid.simple: When true and this button is visible, the mouse is NOT locked to the center of the screen (unless right mouse is held). Useful so players in first person can still move the mouse to click a menu.
kid.example:
local closeButton = script.Parent
closeButton.Modal = true -- free the mouse while this menu is open

m.d:
A HapticEffect that the engine plays when the button enters its pressed state. Assign a HapticEffect to give press or click feedback; leave it unset for no press haptics.

The effect plays through the standard HapticService mixer, so whether the player actually feels vibration depends on their device and haptic settings. This property defaults to nil (no effect).
m.s: A `Class.HapticEffect` instance that will play when the `Class.GuiButton` is being pressed.

kid.simple: A HapticEffect (vibration) that plays when the button is pressed. Leave empty for no vibration.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
local buzz = Instance.new("HapticEffect")
buzz.Type = Enum.HapticEffectType.UIClick
buzz.Parent = button
button.PressHapticEffect = buzz

m.d:
When set to true, the button renders in a highlighted "selected" state instead of its normal idle appearance. This property defaults to false, and the engine never changes it automatically; set it yourself to mark a button as selected.

Selected only has a visual effect on the legacy ButtonStyle presets (the Roblox* styles) with AutoButtonColor enabled, where it swaps in the button's highlighted image. It has no effect under the default Style of Custom. It is unrelated to gamepad and controller UI navigation; the currently focused element is tracked separately by SelectedObject.
m.s: A boolean property which indicates whether the object has been selected.

kid.simple: When true, the button shows a highlighted 'selected' look, but only for the old built-in Roblox button styles. With the normal Custom style it does nothing visible. Roblox never changes it for you.
kid.example:
local tabButton = script.Parent
tabButton.Selected = true
kid.gotcha: It has nothing to do with gamepad selection. That is GuiService.SelectedObject.

m.d:
Sets the button's overall appearance from a fixed set of ButtonStyle presets. The default value is Custom, which applies no built-in styling and lets you control the button's appearance entirely through properties such as BackgroundColor3 and, for an ImageButton, its images.

A legacy method of applying a fixed set of Roblox-themed button styles. The remaining presets (RobloxButton, RobloxButtonDefault, RobloxRoundButton, RobloxRoundDefaultButton, and RobloxRoundDropdownButton) render Roblox-themed button art. New interfaces should keep Custom and style the button directly. This property defaults to ButtonStyle.Custom.
m.s: Sets the style of the `Class.GuiButton` based on a list of pre-determined styles.

kid.simple: Picks one of Roblox's old built-in button looks. The default, Custom, lets you style the button yourself with BackgroundColor3 and friends, which is what new games should do.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.Style = Enum.ButtonStyle.Custom -- style it yourself

m.d:
Fires when a left click press-and-release is detected on desktop, touch release is detected on mobile, or A/cross is activated in UI navigation mode on console. The first time this method is called, clickCount will start at 0.

As this event doesn't fire on the server, it should only be used in a LocalScript, or in a Script with RunContext of RunContext.Client.
m.s: Fires when the button is activated.

p.s: An InputObject representing the user input that activated the button.
The number of consecutive rapid activations, starting at 0 for the first activation and incrementing with each subsequent activation within quick succession of the previous one.

kid.simple: THE button-pressed event. Fires on a full mouse click, a finger tap on mobile, or the A button on a controller. Gives you the InputObject and a clickCount (starts at 0) you can use to spot quick repeated clicks.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.Activated:Connect(function(inputObject, clickCount)
	print("Pressed! clickCount =", clickCount)
end)
kid.gotcha: Doesn't fire on the server. Use it in a LocalScript.

m.d:
This event fires when the user's mouse fully left clicks the GuiButton.

In regards to clicking, the mouse must be in bounds of the GuiButton and the mouse button must be pressed down and up again before this event fires. If the mouse leaves the bounds of the GuiButton and is released, the event will not fire. If you would like to avoid this limitation, you can use MouseButton1Down and MouseButton1Up; these events are similar but will fire whenever the user presses their left mouse button down or up, respectively.
m.s: Fires when the user's mouse fully left clicks the `Class.GuiButton`.

kid.simple: Fires on a full LEFT mouse click: press down and let go while still on the button. If the mouse slides off before letting go, it doesn't fire.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.MouseButton1Click:Connect(function()
	print("Left clicked")
end)
kid.gotcha: Prefer Activated, which also works on touch and gamepad.

m.d:
This event fires when the user presses their left mouse button down on the GuiButton.

For an event requiring the user to press and release their left mouse on a GuiButton in order for the event to fire, consider using MouseButton1Click.
m.s: Fires when the user presses their left mouse button down on the `Class.GuiButton`.

p.s: The mouse's X screen coordinate in pixels.
The mouse's Y screen coordinate in pixels.

kid.simple: Fires the moment the LEFT mouse button is pressed down on the button (before letting go). Gives mouse x and y.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.MouseButton1Down:Connect(function(x, y)
	print("Pressing down at", x, y)
end)

m.d:
This event fires when the user releases their left mouse button off of the GuiButton.

For an event requiring the user to press and release their left mouse on a GuiButton in order for the event to fire, consider using MouseButton1Click.
m.s: Fires when the user releases their left mouse button off of the `Class.GuiButton`.

p.s: The mouse's X screen coordinate in pixels.
The mouse's Y screen coordinate in pixels.

kid.simple: Fires when the LEFT mouse button is let go over the button. Gives mouse x and y.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.MouseButton1Up:Connect(function(x, y)
	print("Let go at", x, y)
end)

m.d:
This event fires when the user's mouse fully right clicks the GuiButton.

In regards to clicking, the mouse must be in bounds of the GuiButton and the mouse button must be pressed down and up again before this event fires. If the mouse leaves the bounds of the GuiButton and is released, the event will not fire. If you would like to avoid this limitation, you can use MouseButton2Down and MouseButton2Up; these events are similar but will fire whenever the user presses their right mouse button down or up, respectively.
m.s: Fires when the user's mouse fully right clicks the `Class.GuiButton`.

kid.simple: Fires on a full RIGHT mouse click (press and let go while on the button).
kid.example:
local itemButton = script.Parent
itemButton.MouseButton2Click:Connect(function()
	print("Right clicked - show options menu")
end)
kid.gotcha: Mouse only. SecondaryActivated also covers long-press on touch and gamepad.

m.d:
This event fires when the user presses their right mouse button down on the GuiButton.

For an event requiring the user to press and release their right mouse on a GuiButton in order for the event to fire, consider using MouseButton2Click.
m.s: Fires when the user presses their right mouse button down on the `Class.GuiButton`.

p.s: The mouse's X screen coordinate in pixels.
The mouse's Y screen coordinate in pixels.

kid.simple: Fires the moment the RIGHT mouse button is pressed down on the button. Gives mouse x and y.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.MouseButton2Down:Connect(function(x, y)
	print("Right button down")
end)

m.d:
This event fires when the user releases their right mouse button off of the GuiButton.

For an event requiring the user to press and release their right mouse on a GuiButton in order for the event to fire, consider using MouseButton2Click.
m.s: Fires when the user releases their right mouse button off of the `Class.GuiButton`.

p.s: The mouse's X screen coordinate in pixels.
The mouse's Y screen coordinate in pixels.

kid.simple: Fires when the RIGHT mouse button is let go over the button. Gives mouse x and y.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.MouseButton2Up:Connect(function(x, y)
	print("Right button up")
end)

m.d: Fires when a right-click press-and-release is detected from a mouse, long press is detected on a touch input, R3 is detected from a gamepad, or AltEnter is detected in UI navigation mode using keyboard.
m.s: Fires when the button's "secondary" input is activated.

p.s: The input object representing the alternate activation action.

kid.simple: The 'other action' version of Activated. Fires on right-click with a mouse, a long press on touch, R3 on a gamepad, or Alt+Enter in keyboard UI navigation. Good for 'more options' or 'drop item'.
kid.example:
local itemButton = script.Parent
itemButton.SecondaryActivated:Connect(function(inputObject)
	print("Show more options for this item")
end)

kid.simple: GuiButton is the base for the two clickable UI objects: TextButton and ImageButton. It gives them click events, most importantly Activated, which fires when the button is clicked with a mouse, tapped on a phone, or pressed with the A button on a controller. You never create a GuiButton itself; you create a TextButton or ImageButton.
kid.analogy: GuiButton is like the 'push' part of every doorbell. Some doorbells have a label (TextButton), some have a picture (ImageButton), but they all ring when pressed.
whenToUse: Running code when a player clicks or taps a button (Activated)
Doing something on right-click or long-press (SecondaryActivated)
Turning the automatic hover/press color change on or off (AutoButtonColor)
Letting the mouse move freely while a menu is open in first person (Modal)
kid.where: Client side, inside a ScreenGui, or a SurfaceGui/BillboardGui that is in the player's PlayerGui. Make a TextButton or ImageButton (not a GuiButton). Button code goes in a LocalScript, for example inside the button itself in StarterGui.

terms.abstract: Only used as a base for other types. You never create it yourself.
terms.event: Something that happens, like a click. Use :Connect(function) to run code when it happens.
terms.Activated: The best 'button was pressed' event. It works the same with mouse, touch and gamepad.
terms.multi-platform: Works on computers, phones, tablets and consoles.
terms.LocalScript: A script that runs on the player's own device. Button clicks only happen there, so button code must be in a LocalScript.
terms.server: Roblox's computer that runs the game for everyone. It can't see clicks on UI directly; use a RemoteEvent to tell it.
terms.RemoteEvent: A messenger object that lets a LocalScript send a message to the server (or the other way around).
terms.InputObject: An object that describes one input, such as which mouse button or which finger.
terms.haptic: Vibration you can feel, like a controller or phone buzzing.
terms.mouse lock: When the mouse is stuck in the middle of the screen, like in first-person view or shift-lock.

examples.title: Make a button that does something
examples.place: LocalScript inside a TextButton (inside a ScreenGui in StarterGui)
examples.code:
local button = script.Parent -- the TextButton
local clicks = 0

button.Activated:Connect(function()
	clicks += 1
	button.Text = "Clicked " .. clicks .. " times"
end)
explain: script.Parent is the button, since the LocalScript is inside it.
Activated fires on mouse click, phone tap, and controller A-button press, so one line covers every device.
Each press adds 1 to clicks and updates the button's text.

examples.title: Ask the server to do something when a button is pressed
examples.place: LocalScript inside a TextButton, plus a Script in ServerScriptService, plus a RemoteEvent named "BuySword" in ReplicatedStorage
examples.code:
-- LocalScript inside the TextButton
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
local buySword = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("BuySword")
local button = script.Parent

button.Activated:Connect(function()
	buySword:FireServer() -- tell the server 'I want to buy the sword'
end)

-- Script in ServerScriptService (a separate script!)
-- local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")
-- local buySword = ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("BuySword")
-- buySword.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player)
-- 	print(player.Name, "wants to buy the sword")
-- 	-- check they have enough coins HERE, on the server
-- end)
explain: Buttons only work on the player's device, so the click is detected in a LocalScript.
Things that matter for everyone (coins, items) must be done by the server, so we send a message with a RemoteEvent.
The commented part shows what the server Script looks like. Put it in its own Script in ServerScriptService.
Always check things like 'has enough coins' on the server, because players could cheat on their own device.

gotchas: Clicks never reach a server Script directly. Use a LocalScript, and a RemoteEvent if the server needs to know.
Use Activated instead of MouseButton1Click so your button works on phones and controllers too.
Buttons inside a SurfaceGui or BillboardGui only get clicks if that Gui is in the player's PlayerGui (put it in StarterGui and set Adornee).
If Interactable is false, the button can't be clicked at all.

class/GuiLabel.d: GuiLabel is an abstract class that inherits from GuiObject. It is the base class for ImageLabel and TextLabel. Unlike GuiButton, objects of this type will not register click events, but instead serve as non-interactive labels. It does not implement any further properties, events or methods.
class/GuiLabel.s: An abstract class for non-interactive 2D user interface elements.

class/GuiMain.dep: This deprecated class is the original name of the ScreenGui. It functions identically to the ScreenGui, and should not be used.

class/GuiObject.d:
GuiObject is an abstract class (much like BasePart) for a 2D user interface object. It defines all the properties relating to the display of a graphical user interface (GUI) object such as Size and Position. It also has some useful read‑only properties like AbsolutePosition, AbsoluteSize, and AbsoluteRotation.

To manipulate the layout of GUI objects in special ways, you can use a layout structure such as list/flex or grid, and you can style them beyond their core properties through appearance modifiers.

Although it's possible to detect mouse button events on any GUI object using InputBegan and InputEnded, only ImageButton and TextButton have convenient dedicated events such as Activated to detect click/press.
class/GuiObject.s: An abstract class for all 2D user interface objects.

m.d:
This property determines whether the GuiObject will sink input to 3D space, such as underlying models with a ClickDetector class like DragDetector.

For GuiButton objects (ImageButton and TextButton), this property determines whether Activated fires (AutoButtonColor will still work for those as well). The events InputBegan, InputChanged, and InputEnded work as normal no matter the value of this property.
m.s: Determines whether this UI element sinks input.

kid.simple: Decides whether this UI 'catches' clicks so they don't fall through to 3D things behind it (like a ClickDetector on a part). For buttons, it also decides whether the Activated event fires.
kid.example:
local panel = script.Parent -- a Frame
panel.Active = true -- clicks on this panel won't reach parts behind it
kid.gotcha: For finer control there is the newer InputSink property.

m.d:
This property determines the origin point of a GuiObject, relative to its absolute size. The origin point determines from where the element is positioned (through GuiObject.Position) and from which the rendered GuiObject.Size expands.

See here for illustrated diagrams and details.
m.s: Determines the origin point of a `Class.GuiObject`, relative to its absolute size.

kid.simple: Chooses which point of the object Position puts in place, as fractions of the object's own size from 0 to 1. (0, 0) is the top-left corner (default), (0.5, 0.5) is the center, (1, 1) is the bottom-right. Size also grows outward from this point. For a 200x100 frame, AnchorPoint (0.5, 0.5) means the point 100 pixels in and 50 pixels down.
kid.example:
local frame = script.Parent
-- Perfectly center the frame on the screen
frame.AnchorPoint = Vector2.new(0.5, 0.5)
frame.Position = UDim2.fromScale(0.5, 0.5)
kid.gotcha: Changing AnchorPoint makes the frame jump, because Position now places a different point. Set both together.

m.d:
This property is used to automatically size parent UI objects based on the size of its descendants. You can use this property to dynamically add text and other content to a UI object at edit or run time, and the size will adjust to fit that content.

When AutomaticSize is set to an AutomaticSize value to anything other than None, this UI object may resize depending on its child content.

For more information on how to use this property and how it works, please see here.
m.s: Determines whether resizing occurs based on child content.

kid.simple: Lets the object grow to fit what's inside it, like text that gets longer. Choose X (grow wider), Y (grow taller), XY (both) or None (default). The normal Size then acts as the smallest it can be.
kid.example:
local label = script.Parent -- a TextLabel
label.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(200, 0) -- 200 wide, no minimum height
label.TextWrapped = true
label.AutomaticSize = Enum.AutomaticSize.Y -- grows taller to fit all the text
label.Text = "This is a long message that will wrap onto several lines."
kid.gotcha: Don't use AutomaticSize and TextScaled together on the same label; they fight each other.

m.d: Determines the color of the GuiObject background.
m.s: Determines the color of the `Class.GuiObject` background.
m.dep: This property is deprecated in favor of the Color3 property GuiObject.BackgroundColor3, which should be used in new work instead.

kid.simple: Old — use BackgroundColor3 instead.

m.d:
This property determines the color of a GuiObject background (the fill color). If your element contains text, such as a TextBox, TextButton, or TextLabel, make sure the color of your background contrasts the text's color.

Another property that determines the visual properties of the background is GuiObject.BackgroundTransparency; if this is set to 1, neither the background nor the border will render.

See also BorderColor3.
m.s: Determines the `Class.GuiObject` background color.

kid.simple: The fill color of the object's background rectangle. Pick colors that contrast with any text on top so it's easy to read.
kid.example:
local frame = script.Parent
frame.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(30, 30, 30) -- dark gray

m.d:
This property determines the transparency of the GuiObject background and border. It does not, however, determine the transparency of text if the GUI is a TextBox, TextButton, or TextLabel; text transparency is determined TextBox.TextTransparency, TextButton.TextTransparency, and TextLabel.TextTransparency respectively.

If this property is set to 1, neither the background nor the border will render and the GUI background will be completely transparent.
m.s: Determines the transparency of the `Class.GuiObject` background and border.

kid.simple: How see-through the background (and border) is. 0 = completely solid, 1 = completely invisible, 0.5 = half see-through. It does NOT affect text or images on the object; those have their own transparency.
kid.example:
local label = script.Parent -- a TextLabel
label.BackgroundTransparency = 1 -- hide the box, show only the text
kid.gotcha: Want to hide everything, including text and children? Use Visible = false instead.

m.d: Determines the color of the GuiObject border.
m.s: Determines the color of the `Class.GuiObject` border.
m.dep: This property is deprecated in favor of the Color3 property BorderColor3, which should be used in new work instead.

kid.simple: Old — use BorderColor3 instead.

m.d:
Determines the color of the GuiObject rectangular border (also known as the stroke color). This is separate from the object's GuiObject.BackgroundColor3. You will not be able to see the object's border if its GuiObject.BorderSizePixel property is set to 0.

Note that the UIStroke component allows for more advanced border effects.
m.s: Determines the color of the `Class.GuiObject` border.

kid.simple: The color of the simple rectangle border around the object. You won't see it if BorderSizePixel is 0.
kid.example:
local frame = script.Parent
frame.BorderSizePixel = 3
frame.BorderColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(255, 255, 255) -- white border
kid.gotcha: For rounded or fancier borders, add a UIStroke instead.

m.d:
This property determines in what manner the GuiObject border is laid out relative to its dimensions using the enum of the same name, BorderMode.

Note that UIStroke can override this property and allow for more advanced border effects.
m.s: Determines in what manner the `Class.GuiObject` border is laid out relative to its dimensions.

kid.simple: Decides where the simple border is drawn: Outline (outside the edge, default), Middle (half in, half out), or Inset (inside the edge).
kid.example:
local frame = script.Parent
frame.BorderMode = Enum.BorderMode.Inset -- border stays inside the frame's size

m.d:
This property determines how wide the GuiObject border renders, in pixels. Setting this to 0 disables the border altogether.

Note that UIStroke can override this property and allow for more advanced border effects.
m.s: Determines the pixel width of the `Class.GuiObject` border.

kid.simple: How thick the simple border is, in pixels. 0 means no border at all.
kid.example:
local frame = script.Parent
frame.BorderSizePixel = 0 -- no border, clean look

m.d:
This property determines if the GuiObject will clip (make invisible) any portion of descendant GUI elements that would otherwise render outside the bounds of the rectangle.

Rotation Behavior

When StarterGui.ClipsDescendantsSupportsRotation is enabled, clipping works correctly for rotated shapes. However, clipping by rotated shapes (when the clipping parent itself is rotated) or by rounded corners (UICorner) is not supported.

When StarterGui.ClipsDescendantsSupportsRotation is not enabled and this GuiObject or any ancestor GuiObject has a non‑zero Rotation, this property is ignored and descendant GUI elements will render regardless of this property's value.
m.s: Determines if descendant `Class.GuiObject|GuiObjects` outside of the bounds of a parent GUI element should render.

kid.simple: When true, anything inside this object that sticks out past its edges gets cut off and hidden, like looking through a window frame. Great for health bars and sliding panels.
kid.example:
local window = script.Parent
window.ClipsDescendants = true -- children can't draw outside this frame
kid.gotcha: It doesn't clip to rounded UICorner corners, and it may be ignored if this object or a parent is rotated.

m.d: This indicates whether a GuiObject (and its descendants) can be dragged around the screen.
m.s: Determines whether a `Class.GuiObject` (and its descendants) can be dragged around the screen.
m.dep: This property is deprecated. Use UIDragDetector instead, as it supports more input types and can be better customized.

kid.simple: Old — use a UIDragDetector instead.

m.d: When the player's finger is being tapped and held on the GuiObject, the GuiState of the GuiObject will be set to Press. Similarly, When the player's finger is being released from the GuiObject, the GuiState of the GuiObject will be set to Idle, and when Interactable is turned off on the GuiObject, the GuiState of the GuiObject will be set to NonInteractable.
m.s: Determines whether the player's mouse is being actively pressed on the `Class.GuiObject` or not.

kid.simple: Read-only. Tells you what is happening to this object right now: Idle, Hover, Press, or NonInteractable (when Interactable is false).
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button:GetPropertyChangedSignal("GuiState"):Connect(function()
	print("Button state is now", button.GuiState)
end)

m.d:
Controls whether, and to what degree, the GuiObject sinks input that occurs over it, using InputSink. Sinking input prevents it from passing through to objects behind the element, including 3D objects in the world such as those with a ClickDetector or DragDetector. It defaults to InputSink.None, except on GuiButton objects (ImageButton and TextButton), where it defaults to InputSink.Activate.

  • InputSink.None — the object does not sink input on its own.
  • InputSink.Activate — the object sinks the mouse-button and touch press/release input used to activate it, but lets other input (such as mouse movement) pass through.
  • InputSink.All — the object sinks all input that occurs over it.

This property is a more granular successor to the boolean Active property, which can only sink all input or none. The InputBegan, InputChanged, and InputEnded events fire regardless of this property's value.
m.s: Controls whether, and how, the `Class.GuiObject` sinks input that occurs over it.

kid.simple: A more detailed version of Active. Decides how much input this object catches so it doesn't go through to things behind it. None = catches nothing, Activate = catches presses and taps used to click it (the default for buttons), All = catches everything over it.
kid.example:
local panel = script.Parent
panel.InputSink = Enum.InputSink.All -- nothing passes through this panel

m.d:
Determines whether the GuiButton can be interacted with or not, or if the GuiState of the GuiObject is changing or not.

On a GuiButton:

  • When the Interactable setting on the GuiButton is set to false, the GuiButton will no longer be able to be pressed or clicked, and the GuiState will be constantly set to NonInteractable.
  • When the Interactable setting on the GuiButton is set to true, the GuiButton will behave normally again and the GuiState will behave normally.

On a GuiObject:

  • When the Interactable setting on the GuiButton is set to false, the GuiState will be constantly set to NonInteractable.
  • When the Interactable setting on the GuiButton is set to true, the GuiState will behave normally again.
m.s: Determines whether the `Class.GuiButton` can be interacted with or not, or if the `Enum.GuiState|GuiState` of the `Class.GuiObject` is changing or not.

kid.simple: When false, a button can't be clicked or pressed at all, and GuiState stays NonInteractable. Handy for greying out a 'Buy' button the player can't afford.
kid.example:
local buyButton = script.Parent -- a TextButton
buyButton.Interactable = false -- can't be clicked right now
buyButton.BackgroundTransparency = 0.5 -- look faded so the player knows

m.d:
This property controls the sorting order of the GuiObject when using a UIGridStyleLayout (such as UIListLayout or UIPageLayout) with SortOrder set to SortOrder.LayoutOrder. It has no functionality if the object does not have a sibling UI layout structure.

GuiObjects are sorted in ascending order where lower values take priority over higher values. Objects with equal values fall back to the order they were added in.

If you are unsure if you'll need to add an element between two existing elements in the future, it's a good practice to use multiples of 100 (0, 100, 200, etc.). This ensures a large gap of layout order values which you can use for elements ordered in-between other elements.

See also ZIndex which determines the object's rendering order instead of sorting order.
m.s: Controls the sort order of the `Class.GuiObject` when used with a `Class.UIGridStyleLayout`.

kid.simple: A number that decides the order this object appears in when a UIListLayout, UIGridLayout or UIPageLayout is arranging it, and that layout's SortOrder is LayoutOrder. Lower numbers come first. Equal numbers fall back to the order they were added.
kid.example:
-- Three buttons inside a Frame that has a UIListLayout with SortOrder = LayoutOrder
local frame = script.Parent
frame.PlayButton.LayoutOrder = 100     -- first
frame.SettingsButton.LayoutOrder = 200 -- second
frame.QuitButton.LayoutOrder = 300     -- third
kid.gotcha: Does nothing without a layout object next to it. Use gaps like 100, 200, 300 so you can slip something in between later (150). Not the same as ZIndex, which is about what's drawn on top.

m.d:
This property sets the GuiObject selected when the user moves the gamepad selector downward. If this property is empty, moving the gamepad downward will not change the selected GUI.

Moving the gamepad selector downward sets the GuiService.SelectedObject to this object unless the GUI is not Selectable. Note that this property can be set to a GUI element even if it is not Selectable, so you should ensure that the value of a GUI's selectable property matches your expected behavior.

See also NextSelectionUp, NextSelectionLeft, and NextSelectionRight.
m.s: Sets the `Class.GuiObject` which will be selected when the gamepad selector is moved downward.

kid.simple: For gamepad players: which UI object gets selected when they press DOWN while this one is selected. Empty means pressing down won't move here.
kid.example:
local playButton = script.Parent.PlayButton
local quitButton = script.Parent.QuitButton
playButton.NextSelectionDown = quitButton

m.d:
This property sets the GuiObject selected when the user moves the gamepad selector to the left. If this property is empty, moving the gamepad to the left will not change the selected GUI.

Moving the gamepad selector to the left sets the GuiService.SelectedObject to this object unless the GUI is not Selectable. Note that this property can be set to a GUI element even if it is not Selectable, so you should ensure that the value of a GUI's selectable property matches your expected behavior.

See also NextSelectionUp, NextSelectionDown, and NextSelectionRight.
m.s: Sets the `Class.GuiObject` which will be selected when the gamepad selector is moved to the left.

kid.simple: For gamepad players: which UI object gets selected when they press LEFT while this one is selected.
kid.example:
local rightButton = script.Parent.RightButton
rightButton.NextSelectionLeft = script.Parent.LeftButton

m.d:
This property sets the GuiObject selected when the user moves the gamepad selector to the right. If this property is empty, moving the gamepad to the right will not change the selected GUI.

Moving the gamepad selector to the right sets the GuiService.SelectedObject to this object unless the GUI is not Selectable. Note that this property can be set to a GUI element even if it is not Selectable, so you should ensure that the value of a GUI's selectable property matches your expected behavior.

See also NextSelectionUp, NextSelectionDown, and NextSelectionLeft.
m.s: Sets the `Class.GuiObject` which will be selected when the gamepad selector is moved to the right.

kid.simple: For gamepad players: which UI object gets selected when they press RIGHT while this one is selected.
kid.example:
local leftButton = script.Parent.LeftButton
leftButton.NextSelectionRight = script.Parent.RightButton

m.d:
This property sets the GuiObject selected when the user moves the gamepad selector upward. If this property is empty, moving the gamepad upward will not change the selected GUI.

Moving the gamepad selector upward sets the GuiService.SelectedObject to this object unless the GUI is not Selectable. Note that this property can be set to a GUI element even if it is not Selectable, so you should ensure that the value of a GUI's selectable property matches your expected behavior.

See also NextSelectionDown, NextSelectionLeft, NextSelectionRight.
m.s: Sets the `Class.GuiObject` which will be selected when the gamepad selector is moved upward.

kid.simple: For gamepad players: which UI object gets selected when they press UP while this one is selected.
kid.example:
local quitButton = script.Parent.QuitButton
quitButton.NextSelectionUp = script.Parent.PlayButton

m.d:
This property determines the GuiObject pixel and scalar position using a UDim2. Position is centered around the object's GuiObject.AnchorPoint.

The scalar position is relative to the size of the parent GUI element, if any.

The pixel portions of the UDim2 value are the same regardless of the parent GUI's size. The values represent the position of the object in pixels. An object's actual pixel position can be read from the GuiBase2d.AbsolutePosition property.
m.s: Determines the pixel and scalar position of the `Class.GuiObject`.

kid.simple: Where the object goes inside its parent, as a UDim2: (X Scale, X Offset, Y Scale, Y Offset). Scale is a fraction of the parent's size, Offset is extra pixels. On a 1000x600 screen, UDim2.new(0.5, 20, 0, 100) puts the object's AnchorPoint at x = 0.5 x 1000 + 20 = 520 and y = 0 x 600 + 100 = 100.
kid.example:
local frame = script.Parent
frame.Position = UDim2.new(0.5, 20, 0, 100) -- 50% across + 20 px, 100 px down
frame.Position = UDim2.fromScale(0.1, 0.1)  -- 10% across, 10% down
frame.Position = UDim2.fromOffset(50, 50)   -- exactly 50 px across, 50 px down
kid.gotcha: Position places the AnchorPoint, which is the top-left corner unless you changed it. Inside a list or grid layout, Position is ignored.

m.d: This property determines the number of degrees by which the GuiObject is rotated. Rotation is relative to the center of the object, not the AnchorPoint, meaning you cannot change the point of rotation. Additionally, this property is not compatible with ClipsDescendants.
m.s: Determines the number of degrees by which the `Class.GuiObject` is rotated.

kid.simple: Turns the object by this many degrees, clockwise, around its CENTER (not around the AnchorPoint). 90 is a quarter turn.
kid.example:
local arrow = script.Parent -- an ImageLabel of an arrow
arrow.Rotation = 45 -- tilt it diagonally
kid.gotcha: Rotation and ClipsDescendants don't always work well together.

m.d:
This property determines whether the GuiObject can be selected when navigating GUIs using a gamepad.

If this property is true, a GUI can be selected. Selecting a GUI also sets the GuiService.SelectedObject property to that object.

When this is false, the GUI cannot be selected. However, setting this to false when a GUI is selected will not deselect it nor change the value of the GuiService.SelectedObject property.

Add GuiObject.SelectionGained and GuiObject.SelectionLost will not fire for the element. To deselect a GuiObject, you must change the GuiService.SelectedObject property.

This property is useful if a GUI is connected to several GUIs via properties such as this GuiObject.NextSelectionUp, GuiObject.NextSelectionDown, NextSelectionRight, or NextSelectionLeft. Rather than change all of the properties so that the Gamepad cannot select the GUI, you can disable its Selectable property to temporarily prevent it from being selected. Then, when you want the gamepad selector to be able to select the GUI, simply re-enable its selectable property.
m.s: Determine whether the `Class.GuiObject` can be selected by a gamepad.

kid.simple: Whether a gamepad player can select (highlight) this object. Turn it off to temporarily skip a button during gamepad navigation.
kid.example:
local lockedButton = script.Parent
lockedButton.Selectable = false -- gamepad selection skips it

m.d:
This property overrides the default selection adornment used for gamepads.

Note that the chosen SelectionImageObject overlays the selected GuiObject with the Size of the image. For best results, you should size the custom SelectionImageObject via the scale UDim2 values to help ensure that the object scales properly over the selected element.

Changing the SelectionImageObject for a GuiObject element only affects that element. To affect all of a user's GUI elements, set the PlayerGui.SelectionImageObject property.

To determine or set which GUI element is selected by the user, you can use the GuiService.SelectedObject property. The player uses the gamepad to select different GUI elements, invoking the NextSelectionUp, NextSelectionDown, NextSelectionLeft, and NextSelectionRight events.
m.s: Overrides the default selection adornment used for gamepads.

kid.simple: Lets you replace the default gamepad highlight around this object with your own UI object (like a glowing frame). Size the custom highlight with Scale so it fits the button.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
local glow = Instance.new("Frame")
glow.Size = UDim2.fromScale(1, 1) -- same size as the button
glow.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(255, 220, 0)
glow.BackgroundTransparency = 0.6
button.SelectionImageObject = glow

m.d: GuiObjects with a lower SelectionOrder are selected earlier than GuiObjects with a higher SelectionOrder when starting the gamepad selection or calling GuiService:Select() on an ancestor. This property does not affect directional navigation. Default value is 0.
m.s: The order of `Class.GuiObject|GuiObjects` selected by the gamepad UI selection.

kid.simple: When gamepad selection first starts (or GuiService:Select is called on a parent), objects with a lower SelectionOrder get picked first. Default is 0. It doesn't change what happens when the player presses a direction.
kid.example:
local playButton = script.Parent.PlayButton
playButton.SelectionOrder = -1 -- picked before buttons with 0

m.d:
This property determines the GuiObject scalar and pixel size using a UDim2.

The scalar size is relative to the size of the parent GUI element, if any.

The pixel portions of the UDim2 value are the same regardless of the parent GUI's size. The values represent the size of the object in pixels. An object's actual pixel size can be read from the GuiBase2d.AbsoluteSize property.

If the GuiObject has a parent, its size along each axis is also influenced by the parent's SizeConstraint.
m.s: Determines the pixel and scalar size of the `Class.GuiObject`.

kid.simple: How big the object is, as a UDim2: (X Scale, X Offset, Y Scale, Y Offset). Scale is a fraction of the PARENT's size, Offset is extra pixels. Inside a 1000x600 screen, UDim2.new(0.5, 0, 0, 50) is 500 pixels wide and 50 pixels tall. UDim2.fromScale(1, 1) fills the whole parent.
kid.example:
local frame = script.Parent
frame.Size = UDim2.fromScale(0.5, 0.25)  -- half as wide, a quarter as tall as the parent
frame.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(200, 100)  -- exactly 200 x 100 pixels
frame.Size = UDim2.new(1, -20, 0, 40)    -- full width minus 20 px, 40 px tall
kid.gotcha: The real pixel size is in AbsoluteSize. A grid layout or size constraint can override Size.

m.d:
This property sets the Size axes that the GuiObject will be based on, relative to the size of its parent.

This property is useful for creating GUI objects that are meant to scale with either the width or height of a parent object, but not both, effectively preserving the aspect ratio of the object.
m.s: Sets the `Class.GuiObject.Size|Size` axes that the `Class.GuiObject` will be based on, relative to the size of its parent.

kid.simple: Decides which side of the parent the Scale parts of Size follow. RelativeXY (default) uses width for X and height for Y. RelativeXX uses the parent's WIDTH for both, RelativeYY uses the parent's HEIGHT for both. Using one side for both keeps an object's shape (like a perfect square) on any screen.
kid.example:
local square = script.Parent
square.SizeConstraint = Enum.SizeConstraint.RelativeYY
square.Size = UDim2.fromScale(0.2, 0.2) -- 20% of the parent's HEIGHT both ways = always a square
kid.gotcha: A UIAspectRatioConstraint is often an easier way to keep a shape.

m.d: A mixed property of BackgroundTransparency and TextTransparency.
m.s: A mixed property of `Class.GuiObject.BackgroundTransparency|BackgroundTransparency` and `Class.TextLabel.TextTransparency|TextTransparency`.
m.dep: This property is deprecated and indexing it will return BackgroundTransparency.

kid.simple: Old — use BackgroundTransparency (and TextTransparency for text) instead.

m.d:
This property whether the GuiObject and its descendants will be rendered.

The rendering of individual components of a GuiObject can be controlled individually through transparency properties such as GuiObject.BackgroundTransparency, TextLabel.TextTransparency and ImageLabel.ImageTransparency.

When this property is false, the GuiObject will be ignored by layout structures such as UIListLayout, UIGridLayout, and UITableLayout. In other words, the space that the element would otherwise occupy in the layout is used by other elements instead.
m.s: Determines whether the `Class.GuiObject` and its descendants will be rendered.

kid.simple: Whether the object and everything inside it is drawn. false hides it all, and list or grid layouts skip it as if it wasn't there.
kid.example:
local menu = script.Parent
menu.Visible = not menu.Visible -- toggle: show if hidden, hide if shown

m.d:
This property determines the order in which a GuiObject renders relative to others.

By default, GuiObjects render in ascending priority order where those with lower ZIndex values are rendered under those with higher values. You can change the render order within a ScreenGui, SurfaceGui, or BillboardGui by changing the value of its ZIndexBehavior.

If you are unsure if you'll need to add an element between two existing elements in the future, it's a good practice to use multiples of 100 (0, 100, 200, etc.). This ensures a large gap of render order values which you can use for elements layered in-between other elements.

See also LayoutOrder which controls the sorting order of a GuiObject when used with a layout structure such as UIListLayout or UIGridLayout.
m.s: Determines the order in which a `Class.GuiObject` renders relative to others.

kid.simple: A layer number for drawing order. Objects with a higher ZIndex are drawn on top of objects with a lower one. By default it compares siblings (objects with the same parent); a child is always drawn above its parent.
kid.example:
local background = script.Parent.Background
local title = script.Parent.Title
background.ZIndex = 1
title.ZIndex = 2 -- title is drawn on top of the background
kid.gotcha: Use gaps like 100, 200, 300 so you can add layers in between later. Not the same as LayoutOrder.

m.d:
This event fires when a user begins interacting with the GuiObject via a Human-Computer Interface device (Mouse button down, touch begin, keyboard button down, etc).

The UserInputService has a similarly named event that is not restricted to a specific UI element: UserInputService.InputBegan.

This event will always fire regardless of game state.

See also GuiObject.InputEnded and GuiObject.InputChanged.
m.s: Fired when a user begins interacting via a Human-Computer Interface device (Mouse button down, touch begin, keyboard button down, etc).

p.s: An InputObject, which contains useful data for querying user input such as the type of input, state of input, and screen coordinates of the input.

kid.simple: Fires when the player starts any input on this object: a mouse button pressed down, a finger touching it, and similar. It gives you an InputObject that says what kind of input it was. Works on any UI object, not just buttons.
kid.example:
-- LocalScript inside a Frame
local frame = script.Parent
frame.InputBegan:Connect(function(input)
	if input.UserInputType == Enum.UserInputType.MouseButton1 then
		print("Mouse pressed on the frame")
	elseif input.UserInputType == Enum.UserInputType.Touch then
		print("Finger touched the frame")
	end
end)
kid.gotcha: For simple button clicks, GuiButton.Activated is easier and works on every device.

m.d:
This event fires when a user changes how they're interacting via a Human-Computer Interface device (Mouse button down, touch begin, keyboard button down, etc).

The UserInputService has a similarly named event that is not restricted to a specific UI element: UserInputService.InputChanged.

This event will always fire regardless of game state.

See also GuiObject.InputBegan and GuiObject.InputEnded.
m.s: Fired when a user changes how they're interacting via a Human-Computer Interface device (Mouse button down, touch begin, keyboard button down, etc).

p.s: An InputObject, which contains useful data for querying user input such as the type of input, state of input, and screen coordinates of the input.

kid.simple: Fires when an input on this object changes, for example the mouse moving across it or the mouse wheel turning. You get the InputObject so you can check what changed.
kid.example:
local frame = script.Parent
frame.InputChanged:Connect(function(input)
	if input.UserInputType == Enum.UserInputType.MouseMovement then
		print("Mouse moved to", input.Position.X, input.Position.Y)
	end
end)

m.d:
The InputEnded event fires when a user stops interacting via a Human-Computer Interface device (Mouse button down, touch begin, keyboard button down, etc).

The UserInputService has a similarly named event that is not restricted to a specific UI element: UserInputService.InputEnded.

This event will always fire regardless of game state.

See also GuiObject.InputBegan and GuiObject.InputChanged.
m.s: Fired when a user stops interacting via a Human-Computer Interface device (Mouse button down, touch begin, keyboard button down, etc).

p.s: An InputObject, which contains useful data for querying user input such as the UserInputType, UserInputState, and InputObject.Position.

kid.simple: Fires when an input on this object stops: a mouse button let go, a finger lifted, and similar. Pair it with InputBegan to know when something is being held.
kid.example:
local frame = script.Parent
frame.InputEnded:Connect(function(input)
	if input.UserInputType == Enum.UserInputType.MouseButton1 then
		print("Mouse button released")
	end
end)

m.d:
The MouseEnter event fires when a user moves their mouse into a GuiObject element.

Please do not rely on the x and y arguments passed by this event as a fool-proof way to determine where the user's mouse is when it enters a GUI. These coordinates may vary even when the mouse enters the GUI via the same edge - particularly when the mouse enters the element quickly. This is due to the fact the coordinates indicate the position of the mouse when the event fires rather than the exact moment the mouse enters the GUI.

This event fires even when the GUI element renders beneath another element.

If you would like to track when a user's mouse leaves a GUI element, you can use the GuiObject.MouseLeave event.

See Also
  • GuiObject.MouseLeave
  • GuiObject.MouseMoved
  • GuiObject.MouseWheelForward
  • GuiObject.MouseWheelBackward
m.s: Fires when a user moves their mouse into a GUI element.

p.s: The mouse's X screen coordinate in pixels, relative to the top left corner of the screen.
The mouse's Y screen coordinate in pixels, relative to the top left corner of the screen.

kid.simple: Fires when the mouse pointer moves onto this object. It gives the mouse's x and y in pixels. Great for hover effects like highlighting a button.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.MouseEnter:Connect(function(x, y)
	button.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(255, 255, 150) -- light yellow on hover
end)
kid.gotcha: The x and y may be a little off from the exact edge if the mouse moves fast. It also fires even if another UI object is covering this one.

m.d:
The MouseLeave event fires when a user moves their mouse out of a GuiObject element.

Please do not rely on the x and y arguments passed by this event as a fool-proof way to determine where the user's mouse is when it leaves a GUI. These coordinates may vary even when the mouse leaves the GUI via the same edge - particularly when the mouse leaves the element quickly. This is due to the fact the coordinates indicate the position of the mouse when the event fires rather than the exact moment the mouse leaves the GUI.

This event fires even when the GUI element renders beneath another element.

See Also
  • GuiObject.MouseEnter
  • GuiObject.MouseMoved
  • GuiObject.MouseWheelForward
  • GuiObject.MouseWheelBackward
m.s: Fires when a user moves their mouse out of a GUI element.

p.s: The mouse's X screen coordinate in pixels, relative to the top left corner of the screen.
The mouse's Y screen coordinate in pixels, relative to the top left corner of the screen.

kid.simple: Fires when the mouse pointer moves off this object. Use it to undo a hover effect.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.MouseLeave:Connect(function(x, y)
	button.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(255, 255, 255) -- back to white
end)

m.d:
Fires whenever a user moves their mouse while it is inside a GuiObject element. It is similar to Mouse.Move, which fires regardless whether the user's mouse is over a GUI element.

Note, this event fires when the mouse's position is updated, therefore it will fire repeatedly while being moved.

The x and y arguments indicate the updated screen coordinates of the user's mouse in pixels. These can be useful to determine the mouse's location on the GUI, screen, and delta since the mouse's previous position if it is being tracked in a global variable.

The code below demonstrates how to determine the Vector2 offset of the user's mouse relative to a GUI element. AbsolutePosition is measured inside the screen's GUI inset, while the x and y arguments of this event are screen coordinates that include it, so the sample calls GetGuiInset() to reconcile the two spaces instead of assuming a fixed inset size.

local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local GuiService = game:GetService("GuiService")

local CustomScrollingFrame = script.Parent
local SubFrame = CustomScrollingFrame:FindFirstChild("SubFrame")

local mouse = Players.LocalPlayer:GetMouse()

local function getPosition(X, Y)
    local topLeftInset = GuiService:GetGuiInset()

    local gui_X = CustomScrollingFrame.AbsolutePosition.X
    local gui_Y = CustomScrollingFrame.AbsolutePosition.Y

    local pos = Vector2.new(math.abs(X - gui_X), math.abs(Y - gui_Y - topLeftInset.Y))
    print(pos)
end

CustomScrollingFrame.MouseMoved:Connect(getPosition)

Note that this event may not fire exactly when the user's mouse enters or exits a GUI element. Therefore, the x and y arguments may not match up perfectly to the coordinates of the GUI's edges.

See Also
  • GuiObject.MouseEnter
  • GuiObject.MouseLeave
  • GuiObject.MouseWheelForward
  • GuiObject.MouseWheelBackward
m.s: Fires whenever a user moves their mouse while it is inside a GUI element.

p.s: The mouse's X screen coordinate in pixels, relative to the top left corner of the screen.
The mouse's Y screen coordinate in pixels, relative to the top left corner of the screen.

kid.simple: Fires again and again while the mouse moves around inside this object. Gives the mouse's x and y in screen pixels.
kid.example:
local frame = script.Parent
frame.MouseMoved:Connect(function(x, y)
	print("Mouse at", x, y)
end)
kid.gotcha: x and y include the top bar area, but AbsolutePosition doesn't, so subtract GuiService:GetGuiInset() if you compare them.

m.d:
The WheelBackward event fires when a user scrolls their mouse wheel back when the mouse is over a GuiObject element. It is similar to Mouse.WheelBackward, which fires regardless whether the user's mouse is over a GUI element.

This event fires merely as an indicator of the wheel's backward movement. This means that the x and y mouse coordinate arguments don't change as a result of this event. These coordinates only change when the mouse moves, which can be tracked by the GuiObject.MouseMoved event.

See Also

  • GuiObject.MouseLeave
  • GuiObject.MouseMoved
  • GuiObject.MouseWheelForward

p.s: The mouse's X screen coordinate in pixels, relative to the top left corner of the screen.
The mouse's Y screen coordinate in pixels, relative to the top left corner of the screen.

kid.simple: Fires when the player scrolls the mouse wheel back (toward themselves) while the mouse is over this object.
kid.example:
local zoomBox = script.Parent
zoomBox.MouseWheelBackward:Connect(function(x, y)
	print("Scrolled back - zoom out")
end)

This event fires merely as an indicator of the wheel's forward movement. This means that the X and Y mouse coordinate arguments do not change as a result of this event. These coordinates only change when the mouse moves, which can be tracked by the GuiObject.MouseMoved event.

p.s: The mouse's X screen coordinate in pixels, relative to the top left corner of the screen.
The Y coordinate of the user's mouse.

kid.simple: Fires when the player scrolls the mouse wheel forward (away from themselves) while the mouse is over this object.

local zoomBox = script.Parent

m.d:
This event fires when the Gamepad selector starts focusing on the GuiObject.

If you want to check from the Gamepad select stops focusing on the GUI element, you can use the GuiObject.SelectionLost event.

When a GUI gains selection focus, the value of the SelectedObject property also changes to the that gains selection. To determine which GUI gained selection, check the value of this property.
m.s: Fired when the GuiObject is being focused on with the Gamepad selector.

kid.simple: Fires when a gamepad player's selection highlight moves onto this object.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.SelectionGained:Connect(function()
	button.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(0, 170, 255)
end)

m.d:
This event fires when the Gamepad selector stops focusing on the GuiObject.

If you want to check from the Gamepad select starts focusing on the GUI element, you can use the GuiObject.SelectionGained event.

When a GUI loses selection focus, the value of the SelectionObject property changes either to nil or to the GUI element that gains selection focus. To determine which GUI gained selection, or if no GUI is selected, check the value of this property.
m.s: Fired when the Gamepad selector stops focusing on the GuiObject.

kid.simple: Fires when a gamepad player's selection highlight moves off this object.
kid.example:
local button = script.Parent
button.SelectionLost:Connect(function()
	button.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(255, 255, 255)
end)

m.d: This event fires after a brief moment when the player holds their finger on the UI element using a touch-enabled device. It fires with a table of Vector2 that describe the relative screen positions of the fingers involved in the gesture. In addition, it fires multiple times: UserInputState.Begin after a brief delay, UserInputState.Change if the player moves their finger during the gesture, and finally UserInputState.End. The delay is platform dependent; in Studio it is a little longer than one second.
m.s: Fires when the player starts, continues and stops long-pressing the UI element.

p.s: An array of Vector2 that describe the relative positions of the fingers involved in the gesture.

A UserInputState that describes the state of the gesture:

  • Begin fires once at the beginning of the gesture (after the brief delay)
  • Change fires if the player moves their finger while pressing down
  • End fires once at the end of the gesture when they release their finger.

kid.simple: On touch screens: fires when the player holds a finger on this object for a moment. It fires with state Begin, then Change if the finger moves, then End when it lets go. Gives a table of finger positions and the state.
kid.example:
local card = script.Parent
card.TouchLongPress:Connect(function(touchPositions, state)
	if state == Enum.UserInputState.Begin then
		print("Long press started - show item details")
	end
end)

m.d:
This event fires when the player moves their finger on the UI element using a touch-enabled device. It fires shortly before GuiObject.TouchSwipe would, and does not fire with GuiObject.TouchTap. This event is useful for allowing the player to manipulate the position of UI elements on the screen.

This event fires with a table of Vector2 that describe the relative screen positions of the fingers involved in the gesture. In addition, it fires multiple times: UserInputState.Begin after a brief delay, UserInputState.Change when the player moves their finger during the gesture, and finally with UserInputState.End.
m.s: Fires when the player moves their finger on the UI element.

p.s: A Luau array of Vector2 objects, each indicating the position of all the fingers involved in the gesture.
Indicates how far the pan gesture has gone from its starting point.
Indicates how quickly the gesture is being performed in each dimension.
Indicates the UserInputState of the gesture.

kid.simple: On touch screens: fires while the player slides a finger across this object. Gives finger positions, totalTranslation (how far it moved in total, as a Vector2), velocity (how fast), and state. Useful for dragging things around.
kid.example:
local map = script.Parent
map.TouchPan:Connect(function(touchPositions, totalTranslation, velocity, state)
	print("Dragged by", totalTranslation)
end)

m.d:
This event fires when the player uses two fingers to make a pinch or pull gesture on the UI element using a touch-enabled device. A pinch happens when two or more fingers move closer together, and a pull happens when they move apart. This event fires in conjunction with GuiObject.TouchPan. This event is useful for allowing the player to manipulate the scale (size) of UI elements on the screen, and is most often used for zooming features.

This event fires with a table of Vector2 that describe the relative screen positions of the fingers involved in the gesture. In addition, it fires multiple times: UserInputState.Begin after a brief delay, UserInputState.Change when the player moves a finger during the gesture, and finally with UserInputState.End. It should be noted that the scale should be used multiplicatively.
m.s: Fires when the player performs a pinch or pull gesture using two fingers on the UI element.

p.s: A Luau array of Vector2 objects, each indicating the position of all the fingers involved in the pinch gesture.
A float that indicates the difference from the beginning of the pinch gesture.
A float indicating how quickly the pinch gesture is happening.
Indicates the UserInputState of the gesture.

kid.simple: On touch screens: fires when the player pinches two fingers together or spreads them apart on this object. Gives a scale number (bigger than 1 = spreading apart), velocity, and state. Often used for zooming.
kid.example:
local map = script.Parent
map.TouchPinch:Connect(function(touchPositions, scale, velocity, state)
	print("Pinch scale:", scale)
end)
kid.gotcha: Use the scale by multiplying (newSize = startSize * scale), not adding.

m.d:
This event fires when the player uses two fingers to make a pinch or pull gesture on the UI element using a touch-enabled device. Rotation occurs when the angle of the line between two fingers changes. This event fires in conjunction with GuiObject.TouchPan. This event is useful for allowing the player to manipulate the rotation of UI elements on the screen.

This event fires with a table of Vector2 that describe the relative screen positions of the fingers involved in the gesture. In addition, it fires multiple times: UserInputState.Begin after a brief delay, UserInputState.Change when the player moves a finger during the gesture, and finally with UserInputState.End.
m.s: Fires when the player performs a rotation gesture using two fingers on the UI element.

p.s: A Luau array of Vector2 objects, each indicating the position of all the fingers involved in the gesture.
A float indicating how much the rotation has gone from the start of the gesture.
A float that indicates how quickly the gesture is being performed.
Indicates the UserInputState of the gesture.

kid.simple: On touch screens: fires when the player twists two fingers on this object. Gives rotation (how much the twist turned), velocity, and state.
kid.example:
local dial = script.Parent
dial.TouchRotate:Connect(function(touchPositions, rotation, velocity, state)
	print("Twisted by", rotation)
end)

m.d: This event fires when the player performs a swipe gesture on the UI element using a touch-enabled device. It fires with the direction of the gesture (Up, Down, Left or Right) and the number of touch points involved in the gesture. Swipe gestures are often used to change tabs in mobile UIs.
m.s: Fires when the player performs a swipe gesture on the UI element.

p.s: A SwipeDirection indicating the direction of the swipe gesture (Up, Down, Left or Right).
The number of touch points involved in the gesture (usually 1).

kid.simple: On touch screens: fires when the player quickly swipes across this object. Gives the direction (Up, Down, Left, Right) and how many fingers were used. Great for flipping between tabs or pages.
kid.example:
local pages = script.Parent
pages.TouchSwipe:Connect(function(swipeDirection, numberOfTouches)
	if swipeDirection == Enum.SwipeDirection.Left then
		print("Next page")
	end
end)

m.d: This event fires when the player performs a tap gesture on the UI element using a touch-enabled device. A tap is a quick single touch without any movement involved (a longer press would fire GuiObject.TouchLongPress, and moving during the touch would fire GuiObject.TouchPan and/or GuiObject.TouchSwipe). It fires with a table of Vector2 objects that describe the relative positions of the fingers involved in the gesture.
m.s: Fires when the player performs a tap gesture on the UI element.

p.s: An array of Vector2 that describe the relative positions of the fingers involved in the gesture.

kid.simple: On touch screens: fires when the player quickly taps this object without moving their finger. Gives a table of finger positions.
kid.example:
local frame = script.Parent
frame.TouchTap:Connect(function(touchPositions)
	print("Tapped!")
end)
kid.gotcha: For buttons, use GuiButton.Activated so it also works with mouse and gamepad.

kid.simple: GuiObject is the base for every visible 2D UI piece: Frame, TextLabel, TextButton, TextBox, ImageLabel, ImageButton, ScrollingFrame and more. It gives all of them the important stuff: where they are (Position), how big they are (Size), which point they are placed by (AnchorPoint), which one is drawn on top (ZIndex), their background color, and whether they show at all (Visible). Learn these once and you know them for every UI object.
kid.analogy: Think of a bulletin board covered in paper notes. Every note, whether it's a picture, a sticky note, or a button, has a spot on the board, a size, a color, and can be on top of or under other notes. GuiObject is the rules every note follows.
whenToUse: Placing UI on the screen with Position and sizing it with Size
Making one piece of UI draw on top of another with ZIndex
Showing or hiding UI with Visible
Changing background color or making a background see-through
Reacting when the mouse hovers over, or a finger touches, any UI piece
kid.where: Client side, inside a ScreenGui (on the screen), SurfaceGui (on a part's face), or BillboardGui (floating over something in the world). You can't create a plain GuiObject; you create a Frame, TextLabel, and so on. UI code goes in a LocalScript, for example inside StarterGui or in StarterPlayerScripts.

terms.UI / GUI: User Interface / Graphical User Interface: the buttons, menus, health bars and text drawn on top of the game.
terms.UDim2: The kind of value Position and Size use. It holds 4 numbers: X Scale, X Offset, Y Scale, Y Offset. UDim2.new(0.5, 20, 0, 100) means X = 50% + 20 pixels, Y = 0% + 100 pixels.
terms.Scale: A fraction of the PARENT's size, from 0 to 1. 0.5 means 50% (half) of the parent. On a 1000-pixel-wide screen, X Scale 0.5 = 500 pixels. On a 2000-pixel screen it becomes 1000 pixels, so it grows with the screen.
terms.Offset: An exact number of pixels that never changes with screen size. X Offset 20 always means 20 pixels.
terms.parent: The object something is placed inside. A Frame inside a ScreenGui has the ScreenGui as its parent. Scale is measured against the parent's size.
terms.AnchorPoint: The point on the object that Position puts in place. (0, 0) is the top-left corner (the default), (0.5, 0.5) is the exact middle, (1, 1) is the bottom-right corner.
terms.ZIndex: A layer number. Higher numbers are drawn on top of lower numbers, like stacking paper.
terms.pixel: One tiny dot on the screen.
terms.transparency: How see-through something is. 0 = fully solid, 1 = fully invisible, 0.5 = half see-through.
terms.Color3: A color made from red, green and blue. Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0) is bright red.
terms.Vector2: Two numbers together: X (left-right) and Y (up-down).
terms.LocalScript: A script that runs on the player's own device. All UI code goes in LocalScripts, because each player has their own copy of the UI.
terms.event: Something that happens, like a mouse entering a button. You use :Connect(function) to run your code when it happens.
terms.sink input: To 'catch' a click or touch so it doesn't also go through to the 3D world behind the UI.
terms.clip: To cut off and hide the parts that stick outside the edges.
terms.descendant: Anything inside an object: children, grandchildren, and so on.

examples.title: Position and Size: Scale vs Offset with real numbers
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

-- A ScreenGui is the 'canvas' that shows UI on the player's screen
local screenGui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
screenGui.Name = "SizeDemo"
screenGui.Parent = playerGui

-- Offset only: always exactly 200 x 100 pixels, 50 pixels from the left and top
local fixedBox = Instance.new("Frame")
fixedBox.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(200, 100)    -- same as UDim2.new(0, 200, 0, 100)
fixedBox.Position = UDim2.fromOffset(50, 50)  -- same as UDim2.new(0, 50, 0, 50)
fixedBox.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(255, 80, 80)
fixedBox.Parent = screenGui

-- Scale only: always a quarter of the screen wide and tall
local stretchyBox = Instance.new("Frame")
stretchyBox.Size = UDim2.fromScale(0.25, 0.25)   -- 25% of the screen width and height
stretchyBox.Position = UDim2.fromScale(0.7, 0.1) -- starts 70% across, 10% down
stretchyBox.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(80, 160, 255)
stretchyBox.Parent = screenGui

-- Mixed: half the screen wide plus 20 pixels, and exactly 40 pixels tall
local bar = Instance.new("Frame")
bar.Size = UDim2.new(0.5, 20, 0, 40)
bar.Position = UDim2.new(0, 50, 1, -60) -- 50 px from left, 60 px up from the BOTTOM
bar.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(80, 220, 120)
bar.Parent = screenGui
explain: Imagine the screen area is 1000 pixels wide and 600 pixels tall.
fixedBox uses Offset only. It is 200x100 pixels at (50, 50) on every screen, big or small.

stretchyBox uses Scale only. 0.25 of 1000 = 250 pixels wide, 0.25 of 600 = 150 pixels tall. Its left edge is at 0.7 x 1000 = 700 pixels, top edge at 0.1 x 600 = 60 pixels. On a bigger screen it gets bigger too.
bar mixes both. Width = 0.5 x 1000 + 20 = 520 pixels. Height = 0 x 600 + 40 = 40 pixels.

bar's Position Y is (1, -60): Scale 1 means 'the very bottom' (100% down = 600 pixels), then Offset -60 moves it 60 pixels back up, so its top edge is at 540 pixels. This is a great trick for sticking things near the bottom or right edge.
UDim2.fromOffset(x, y) and UDim2.fromScale(x, y) are shortcuts when you only need one kind.

examples.title: Center a frame with AnchorPoint
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

local screenGui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
screenGui.Name = "CenterDemo"
screenGui.Parent = playerGui

local popup = Instance.new("Frame")
popup.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(300, 200)       -- 300 wide, 200 tall
popup.AnchorPoint = Vector2.new(0.5, 0.5)     -- place it by its MIDDLE, not its top-left
popup.Position = UDim2.fromScale(0.5, 0.5)    -- put that middle at the middle of the screen
popup.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(40, 40, 60)
popup.BackgroundTransparency = 0              -- 0 = solid
popup.Parent = screenGui

print("Top-left corner really is at", popup.AbsolutePosition)
explain: Say the screen area is 1000 x 600 pixels. Position (0.5, 0.5) is the point (500, 300), the center of the screen.
Without AnchorPoint (the default is (0, 0), the top-left corner), the frame's TOP-LEFT corner would sit at (500, 300). The frame would hang down and to the right, not centered.

With AnchorPoint (0.5, 0.5), the frame's MIDDLE sits at (500, 300). Half the width (150) goes left and half the height (100) goes up, so the top-left corner ends up at (350, 200). Perfectly centered on any screen size.
AbsolutePosition prints the real top-left corner, (350, 200) on our pretend screen.
Same trick for other spots: AnchorPoint (1, 1) with Position (1, 1) sticks something into the bottom-right corner.

examples.title: Layer things with ZIndex and see-through backgrounds
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local playerGui = Players.LocalPlayer:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

local screenGui = Instance.new("ScreenGui")
screenGui.Parent = playerGui

local back = Instance.new("Frame")
back.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(200, 200)
back.Position = UDim2.fromOffset(100, 100)
back.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0) -- red
back.ZIndex = 1
back.Parent = screenGui

local front = Instance.new("Frame")
front.Size = UDim2.fromOffset(200, 200)
front.Position = UDim2.fromOffset(180, 180) -- overlaps the red one
front.BackgroundColor3 = Color3.fromRGB(0, 0, 255) -- blue
front.BackgroundTransparency = 0.5 -- half see-through, so you can see red behind it
front.ZIndex = 2 -- higher number = drawn on top
front.Parent = screenGui

task.wait(3)
front.Visible = false -- hide the blue frame after 3 seconds
explain: Both frames are siblings (they share the same parent), so ZIndex decides who is on top. Blue has ZIndex 2, red has 1, so blue is drawn over red.
BackgroundTransparency 0.5 makes the blue background half see-through. 0 would be solid, 1 would be completely invisible.
task.wait(3) pauses for 3 seconds, then Visible = false hides the blue frame (and anything inside it).

examples.title: Make a box grow when the mouse hovers over it
examples.place: LocalScript inside a Frame (in a ScreenGui in StarterGui)
examples.code:
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local frame = script.Parent

local normalSize = frame.Size
local bigSize = UDim2.new(normalSize.X.Scale * 1.1, normalSize.X.Offset * 1.1, normalSize.Y.Scale * 1.1, normalSize.Y.Offset * 1.1)
local info = TweenInfo.new(0.15) -- animation takes 0.15 seconds

frame.MouseEnter:Connect(function()
	TweenService:Create(frame, info, {Size = bigSize}):Play()
end)

frame.MouseLeave:Connect(function()
	TweenService:Create(frame, info, {Size = normalSize}):Play()
end)
explain: We remember the frame's starting Size, then make a version 10% bigger.
MouseEnter fires when the mouse moves onto the frame; we smoothly grow it with TweenService.
MouseLeave fires when the mouse moves off; we shrink it back.
Tip: set AnchorPoint to (0.5, 0.5) so it grows from the middle instead of from the top-left corner.

gotchas: UI code belongs in a LocalScript (or a Script with RunContext set to Client). A normal server Script can't see the player's screen or mouse.
Scale is a fraction from 0 to 1, not a percent. 0.5 means half. Typing 50 into Scale means 50 times the parent size, way off the screen.
Offset-only UI looks tiny on big monitors and huge on small phones. Use Scale for things that should fit any screen, and Offset for small fixed things like padding.
Scale is measured against the PARENT, not always the whole screen. A child frame with Size (0.5, 0.5) inside a 200x200 frame is 100x100 pixels.
AnchorPoint changes which point Position sets. If something looks shifted, check AnchorPoint before changing Position.
ZIndex only compares siblings by default (ZIndexBehavior Sibling). Children are always drawn on top of their parent, no matter their ZIndex.
BackgroundTransparency 1 hides the background AND the border, but not text or images. Use Visible = false to hide the whole thing and everything inside it.
LayoutOrder and ZIndex are different: LayoutOrder decides the order in a list or grid layout, ZIndex decides what is drawn on top.

m.d:
Gets the player's preferred text size as an PreferredTextSize value of Medium (default), Large, Larger, or Largest. This property maps to the Text Size setting available to players from the Roblox and in‑game Settings menus, and it can be combined with Object.GetPropertyChangedSignal() to detect text size setting changes for purposes of adjusting UI.

When working with UI elements, note the following behaviors:

  • Text that is constrained to a minimum and/or maximum size through a UITextSizeConstraint will not shrink below or expand above the set MinTextSize/MaxTextSize, regardless of the player's text size setting.

  • When TextScaled is enabled for a TextLabel or TextButton, the element's text will not be scaled by the PreferredTextSize value.

  • UI elements with AutomaticSize enabled will shrink/grow as PreferredTextSize decreases/increases (element bounds will resize to fit the resized text).

  • When TextWrapped is enabled for a TextLabel or TextButton, the element's text will wrap to additional lines as PreferredTextSize increases, within limits of the element's absolute size.

  • The results returned by TextService:GetTextSize() and TextService:GetTextBoundsAsync() honor changes related to PreferredTextSize.
m.s: Gets the player's preferred text size as an `Enum.PreferredTextSize` value.

m.d:
Gets the player's preferred transparency as a number between 0 and 1. This property maps to the Background Transparency setting available to players from the Roblox and in‑experience Settings menus, and it can be combined with Object.GetPropertyChangedSignal() to detect transparency setting changes for purposes of adjusting UI.

A value of 1 (default) indicates the player prefers the default background transparency, while a value of 0 indicates the player prefers fully opaque (non‑transparent) background transparency for improved readability and contrast. Multiplying a UI element's BackgroundTransparency with PreferredTransparency is the recommended approach, such that backgrounds become more opaque as PreferredTransparency approaches 0.
m.s: Gets the player's preferred transparency as a number between `0` and `1`.

m.d: Functions similarly to GuiService:AddSelectionParent(), but you can give it a tuple of GuiObject that you want to be contained in the group.
m.s: **AddSelectionTuple** works similarly to `Class.GuiService:AddSelectionParent()`, but you can give it a tuple of `Class.GuiObject` that you want to be contained in the group. Beware that the second argument is _not_ a table, but rather the first of several `Class.GuiObject` in the tuple. To pass the contents of a table, use `unpack`/`table.unpack`: ```lua local frame = script.Parent -- Passing various GuiObject individually GuiService:AddSelectionTuple("InventoryButtons", frame.Sort, frame.Trash, frame.Drop) -- Unpacking a table of GuiObject (unpack/table.unpack are equivalent) local inventoryButtons = { frame.Sort, frame.Trash, frame.Drop } GuiService:AddSelectionTuple("InventoryButtons", unpack(inventoryButtons)) ```

m.d:
Displays a notification built from the notificationInfo dictionary using Roblox's native notification UI, and returns a unique identifier string for the notification. The following fields of notificationInfo are recognized:

Field Type Description
Title string The notification's title text.
Text string The notification's body text.
Icon string An image asset to display with the notification.
Buttons {[ButtonInfo]} An array of button definitions. Each entry is a table with a Text (string), a ButtonType (Enum.NotificationButtonType), and an OnActivated (function) callback invoked when the button is pressed.
OnDisplay function Invoked when the notification is shown.
OnDismiss function Invoked when the notification is dismissed.

The returned identifier can be passed to DismissNotification() to dismiss the notification programmatically; an empty string is returned if the notification could not be queued.
m.s: Displays a notification described by `notificationInfo` and returns a unique identifier for it.

p.s: A dictionary describing the notification. Recognized fields are Title (string), Text (string), Icon (string), Buttons (an array of button tables, each with a Text string, a ButtonType NotificationButtonType value, and an OnActivated callback), and OnDisplay/OnDismiss callback functions.

r.s: A unique identifier string for the notification, which can be passed to DismissNotification(). Returns an empty string if the notification could not be queued.
